newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Clinton leads world powers in signing nuke treaty.
newsitem.headline: Clinton leads world powers in signing nuke treaty.

text.p: The world's nuclear powers formally commit themselves on Tuesday to end the Cold War legacy of atomic explosions in the atmosphere, underground or any other part of the environment.

President Bill Clinton leads the signing ceremony of the landmark although flawed Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty followed by at least 55 nations throughout the day, with others pledged to sign in the weeks ahead.

The foreign ministers of China, France, Russia and Britain, representing the other four known nuclear powers sign immediately after Clinton. So does Japan's Ryutaro Hashimoto, prime minister of the only country scarred by Second World War nuclear attacks on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
Australia too is among the early signers, securing its place by a vigorous campaign that resulted in 158 states backing a Sept. 9 General Assembly resolution opening the treaty for signature.

But the treaty requires 44 nations with a nuclear potential to ratify it through their national legislatures before it goes into force. India, whose signature is necessary, has vowed never to sign "this unequal treaty, not now, not later" until the atomic powers devise a timetable for destroying their nuclear arsenals.
New Delhi also is worried about China's nuclear capability and its rival neighbour, Pakistan, which some suspect of having a covert nuclear and missile programme supplied by Beijing.
Currently, the United States and Russia each deploy over 7,000 warheads compared to France with 512, Britain with 464 and China with 284.

Nevertheless, most legal scholars believe that any state that signs the treaty is obligated to abide by it. At minimum the document is expected to create an international norm that would make testing a near moral impossibility.
And despite computer testing, most experts say that without explosions, new developments would be paltry.

"The treaty fulfils a dream first espoused by President Dwight Eisenhower and given life by President John Kennedy, with the limited test ban treaty," a White House official said. "President Clinton will emphasise that it moves us significantly away from the nuclear precipice."
In addition to the five acknowledged nuclear powers -- India, Pakistan and Israel are considered so-called threshold states exploring the development of nuclear arms.

According to a senior U.S. official, Clinton, if re-elected. will present the treaty to the Senate for ratification early in 1997. But neither the United States nor any of the other eight countries will deposit papers of ratification until the other seven are ready to do so.

Clinton is credited with giving the negotiations on a test ban an impetus by dropping initial U.S. demands that countries could opt out of the treaty after 10 years and banning low-yield tests that some Pentagon and other officials wanted.
But the United States is faulted for caving in to demands from Britain, Russia and China that India and others needed to approve the treaty before it could go into force.

"Countries like Britain wanted to turn the attention away from the nuclear states to countries like India, which haven't deployed the bomb, because they themselves were not really reconciled to giving up testing," said Dan Plesch of the British-American Security Information Council, a private research group.
But he said that with Clinton's re-election on Nov. 5 a near certainty they had no choice but to follow Washington and keep the test ban in place.

All five declared nuclear weapons states have imposed voluntary moratoriums on testing. The United States, Russia and Britain stopped testing between 1990 and 1992 while France and China ended blasts only several months ago.
The United States has conducted 1,030 explosions since its first in the New Mexico desert in 1945, followed by Russia with 715, France with 210 and Britain and China with 45 each.
